newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond volatilities bounce slightly.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond volatilities bounce slightly.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options bounced slightly after being pushed down aggressively earlier in the week, dealers said.
However, activity was slow as underlying bond prices fluctuated narrowly around Wednesday's closing levels.
"Volatility came down a little bit too quick," said a brokerage firm trader at the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT).
In late Thursday business, implied volatilities for CBOT January and March T-bond futures options were up about 0.2 point each from Wednesday to around 9.6 and 10.0 percent respectively.
Still, traders noted that volatilities were likely to stay under pressure for a while due to concerns over time-decay for the upcoming weekend and next week's Thanksgiving Day.

"We don't have anything on the horizon that's going to keep volatility bid," the CBOT trader said. "We have no numbers, no Fed (Federal Reserve) meeting. We're dealing with a really quiet time in the market."

With little fear of inflation at the moment, the market could stay quiet until the November U.S. employment report and the first batches of holiday retail sales data due early next month, traders said.
Fixed income markets could rally if those numbers show signs of a slowing economy, but in the meantime the shorter end of the yield curve was particularly likely to be stagnant.
"The short end of the market is going to have a hard time moving higher without new data," a Eurodollar trader for a brokerage firm at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) said.
Implied volatilities for CME March and June Eurodollar futures options were steady at 11.4 and 15.2 percent as underlying futures moved in narrow ranges of three to four basis points.
Traders said options volume was not bad considering the dull futures market.
Spread trades involving purchases of in-the-money strikes were a popular strategy because they are relatively immune to time decay, and several large deals were done.
A large investment bank was seen buying 3,000 contracts of March 94.25/94.50 put spread and a Chicago firm bought 2,000 legs of January 94.25/94.50 call spread in a one-by-two ratio.
